newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asian corn buyers scarce, jitters on bull trend.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian corn buyers scarce, jitters on bull trend.

text.p: Current high corn prices are causing nervous sellers to wonder when the bullish trend will reverse, while the prospects of Chinese exports are still dim, Southeast Asian grain trade sources said on Thursday.

"Sentiment in the market continued firm after the release of the USDA (United States Department of Agriculture) crop data last week and there is still room for prices to edge higher, but players are moving on a hand to mouth basis," one trader said. "Buyers are relaxed but sellers are concerned over when prices could start to fall as buying interest is scarce."
The March and May corn futures contracts on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) were indicated at around $2.73-$2.74 a bushel at the close of trade on Wednesday.
"Prices could possibly move down to $2.50 when players start to liquidate their positions once there is a sign of any price fall," the trader said.

While the corn market is also stirring with rumours about the possible export of up to two million tonnes of Chinese corn, traders in Singapore were sceptical that the exports would come onto the market soon.
"The exports from China remain unclear," one said.
"I think the Chinese exporters have to clear some administrative hurdles before anything can happen," he said.
"Even if the authorities have approved the exports, I think it will only happen after the Chinese New year holidays."
The Chinese Lunar New Year falls on February 7 and could stretch up to 15 days in China.
"Because of this, most Asian markets will be quiet and activities have already started to slow," said another trader.
"Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia are mostly well-covered and these countries are relying on their domestic supplies to satisfy demand," he said.

"Indonesia had overbought (corn) when high prices last June triggered a buying spree stretching eight to nine months ahead. The government was also cornering the buyers to purchase the local crop," the trader said.

"In addition, the longer term price outlook remains uncertain and players don't want to take risks by taking any supplies, lest the price trend changes either way," he added. One trader said there was no sign of any business in Argentine corn this week. Quotes from this origin were hovering around $130-$135 a tonne C&F, little moved from last week.
The soybean market has been steady and activity lacklustre.
One trader said Malaysia has "a position open for February" to cover 30,000 tonnes of soybeans.
The market's attention is focused on the weather in South American soybean growing areas following surprisingly bullish USDA crop figures last Friday.
With not much in the way of unsold soybean supplies around, the market is "walking on a tight rope", a trader said.
Indian origin soymeal was quoted firmer at around $304 a tonne C&F for February/March shipment compared with last week's quote at $295-$297.
"The market is quiet with not much demand seen around the region," one trader said.
